title: Make Array Elements Equal to Zero
statement:
`nums` is an integer array of length `n` holding at least one `0`. A run begins by choosing a start index `curr` where `nums[curr] == 0`, together with a first direction, left or right. Then these rules apply over and over:

- Once `curr` leaves the array (below `0` or above `n - 1`), the run is over.
- On a `0`, take one step in the current direction (right means `curr + 1`, left means `curr - 1`).
- On a positive value, lower `nums[curr]` by 1, turn around, and take one step in the new direction.

A (start, direction) pair is *valid* if the run leaves every element of `nums` equal to `0`. Return how many valid pairs there are; a start can count twice, once per direction.
notes:
## Intuition

Simulating every start and direction works, since the array is short, but it walks back and forth once for every unit in the array. Look at what the walk does instead: it passes over zeros, and each time it meets a positive value it removes one unit and turns around. So it removes units alternately from the part left of the start and the part right of it, beginning with the side it faces first, and it leaves the array as soon as the side it is heading to is empty. Every value ends at zero exactly when the side faced first holds the same total as the other side, or one more. Only the two totals around each zero matter.

## Approach

1. Compute `total`, the sum of `nums`, and walk left to right keeping `leftSum`, the sum before index `i`.
2. At each zero, the rest is on the right: `rightSum = total - leftSum`.
3. Equal sums: both directions work, add 2. Sums one apart: only the direction toward the larger side works, add 1. Otherwise add nothing.
4. Add `nums[i]` to `leftSum` and move on; finally return `count`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 0, 2, 0, 3]`, `total = 6`.

- `i = 1` is a zero: `leftSum = 1`, `rightSum = 5`, four apart, so nothing.
- `i = 3` is a zero: `leftSum = 3`, `rightSum = 3`, equal, so `count = 2`.

The answer is `2`: start at index 3 going either way.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass for `total` and one for the scan.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- With sums one apart, starting toward the smaller side fails: that side runs dry first and the walk leaves through it while the other side still holds a unit.
- Starts must be zeros; a positive index is never a starting point.
- A balanced zero counts twice, once per direction.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `total` | sum of all values |
| `leftSum` | sum of the values before index `i` |
| `rightSum` | sum of the values after the zero at `i` |
| `count` | valid (start, direction) pairs found so far |

narration.2: Add up every value once; the right side's sum follows from it.
narration.3: leftSum is the sum of the values before index i.
narration.4: count collects the valid (start, direction) pairs.
narration.5: Consider every index as a possible start.
narration.6: Only a zero can be a starting position.
narration.7: Everything not on the left is on the right (nums[i] itself is 0).
narration.8: Equal sides: the alternating removals empty both, whichever way the walk starts...
narration.10: One side holds exactly one unit more: starting toward that side empties both.
narration.11: Only that one direction is valid.
narration.14: Index i now belongs to the left part.
narration.16: Every zero has been checked in both directions.
